html:
Gateway architecture and management

The controller reasons and authorizes; the selected Gateway executes against its host. gateway_core owns shared execution, file/HTTP contracts, jobs, terminals, TLS and controller authentication. Linux (gateway_agent), macOS (gateway_macos) and Windows (gateway_windows) supply platform configuration and supported lifecycle scripts.

The platform app.py facades and available model/executor re-exports are supported entry/import surfaces, even without inbound production imports. Startup scripts invoke python -m gateway_core.serve with the platform app string. Shared gateway_core/models.py owns HTTP and execution event schemas; its serializers omit absent optional observations while preserving explicit false/zero facts. Internal workers use the loopback IPC protocol, separate from authenticated public HTTPS and its optional jobs event stream. Linux fixtures can check shared contracts but cannot certify native macOS/Windows socket, ACL or process-tree behavior.

Gateway Management is a controller UI/API for profiles, selected targets and lifecycle. Profiles are not proof of remote health. Capability snapshots and authenticated refresh make support explicit; execution failures remain authoritative when a host becomes unavailable or a dependency is missing. Connection/session/job identity belongs to its owning service, not to a browser label.

Cross-run historical recovery uses the same Gateway jobs authority for foreground and background execution. POSIX process identity and surviving group members retain live claims; unobservable Windows descendant ownership stays conservative and cannot offer a baseline override. The separate advanced unobservable-owner decision, when unsafe policy is Ask, requires explicit candidate-bound risk confirmation; it never establishes process death. Resource/classifier metadata upgrades through the Gateway RAM jobs authority and is saved by its checkpoint owner. See Gateway state and recovery for ownership, safety fences and offline repair.

For step-by-step availability, pairing, signed HTTP, outbound WSS and disconnect sequences, see Gateway transport flows.

The backend accepts a versioned gateway_selection containing 1–16 unique registry IDs and one explicit primary. The legacy gateway_id remains that primary. Structured scope bypasses nickname inference, survives durable task/schedule dispatch, and is immutable for the run. Native recovery resolves those same IDs again and checks primary and sibling identity pins. Offline targets remain selected; the existing Activity admission reports availability without substituting a target. The Target menu and @gateway palette can select up to 16 Gateways. The first selection of a Gateway adds it; selecting it again removes it. The first selected target is primary; Make primary changes it, and removing it promotes the first remaining selection. The composer shows Multiple gateways · N with removable name chips; an empty selection blocks sending and prompt scheduling. Gateway mentions retain display names in the prompt while structured IDs define scope. Phone Agent options offers the same selection and primary controls.

Browser drafts restore selection per conversation. Offline targets remain selected; deleted or disabled targets require correction before a new submission. A prompt schedule captures the selected IDs and primary when its editor opens. Steering uses the run's original scope and locks selection; future composer choices do not retarget accepted or queued work. Schedule retries keep the original task scope; edits change future runs. Gateway management protects every live sibling reference.

In multi-Gateway runs, shell.command, python.run, file.* and desktop.* accept target with a selected ID. Omit it to use the primary. Each invocation checks the selected host's capabilities and existing permissions; siblings do not inherit the primary's CWD, terminal session or artifact environment. Effects, resources and receipts name the actual target. python.transform remains local to the controller.

The built-in Gateway skill provides controller-side registry management:

Tool Purpose
gateway.list Search registrations by label, ID, host or node, including disabled and unselected Gateways; paginate with next_offset.
gateway.get Read configuration, observed health and current management restrictions for an exact ID.
gateway.create Add an inbound connection using label, host and port; HTTPS and enabled are defaults. A health check follows registration.
gateway.update Change only supplied fields: label, scheme, host, port, node, terminal working directory or enabled state.
gateway.delete Remove a user-created inbound registration. This does not uninstall or stop the remote process.
gateway.health Probe the saved endpoint and refresh health, capabilities and configured TLS trust.

Requests such as “add a Gateway named Lab at lab.example:8787,” “update Lab to use port 9443,” and “delete Lab” use these tools. The agent first resolves the exact registration; ambiguous names require clarification. Mutations and health probes follow the normal permission policy. Settings and the skill share the same service and recheck live dependencies at mutation time, including RAM transaction fencing. An offline endpoint can be registered successfully; the returned status is separate from registration success. After an endpoint update, use gateway.health to verify it.

Connection changes, disabling and deletion remain blocked while tasks, resumable runs, schedules or monitors reference the Gateway, including the requesting run. Clear or retarget that work and manage the registration from another Gateway. Labels remain editable. Startup-configured registrations cannot be deleted here; outbound registrations remain read-only. Management can inspect registrations outside the captured selection, but never expands or retargets that selection. Private transport state and raw capability snapshots are excluded from tool output.

gateway.scope inspects the captured primary and selected Gateways with safe labels, status, platform and capability tags. This scope tool works while hosts are offline and cannot discover additional hosts or expose connection secrets. The skill starts enabled in new product-default capability policies; existing explicit selections remain authoritative. Parallel and dependency Activities use the captured IDs, preserve per-Gateway sequencing and report each target's outcome. Scheduling evaluates concrete resource claims, target sequencing and capacity before permitting overlap. Unavailable targets are never substituted. See resource scheduling for the admission rules.

gateway.copy copies one regular file between selected Gateways through the controller, including inbound/outbound pairs and different target operating systems. Both Gateways must advertise file_transfer. Source read and destination write permissions apply before streaming. The default is no overwrite, SHA-256 verification and mtime preservation. Transfers use binary chunks up to 1 MiB and an atomic destination stage. Older Gateways use compatible base64 chunks, with a 256 KiB limit for versions that do not advertise larger chunks; no file bytes enter model context. The controller's artifact file-size limit and each Gateway's GATEWAY_TRANSFER_MAX_FILE_BYTES limit apply (64 MiB defaults). Use file.copy for copies on one Gateway. A lost commit receipt requires reconciliation before retrying. On owned resume, MG-6 rechecks authority and asks the destination to verify its original staging identity, size and a fresh whole-file hash. Verified recovery produces a completion receipt without retransferring bytes. Precommit interruption aborts the stage safely; a later authorized retry starts from zero. Missing or conflicting evidence remains unknown and cannot authorize blind replay.

Transfer phase metadata shares the native invocation receipt and Gateway RAM transfer domain, with durable transfer fences and asynchronous recovery checkpoints; file bytes never enter either store. Cleanup checks at most 32 registered stages per pass after five idle minutes. It checks exact names, filesystem ownership and identity without recursively scanning user files. Unregistered or replaced files are left alone. Metadata retention is bounded to 256 records per node and up to 24 hours after cleanup; old unverifiable outcomes remain unknown. Directory/tree copy and offset resume are optional extensions that are not implemented: regular files and binary assets are the supported operands, with links and special files rejected.

Existing Activity rows show the selected host. File-copy progress shows source → destination and acknowledged-byte percentage, throttled to once a second plus terminal progress. Saved trace replay preserves target attribution and partial failures. This mechanical work adds no model calls or separate Activity cards.

Monitors remain single-Gateway because each owns one terminal. Their model-led trigger actions inherit that scope; a multi-Gateway selection is rejected explicitly. Use separate monitors for separate hosts. Saved recipe invocations resolve selected Gateway IDs through the same registry before launch; their native run retains the selection and ignores browser transport overrides.

Each remote host must update its own checkout and run its platform installer. Installing the controller does not update a remote Gateway environment. Root installation normally updates the applicable local Gateway environment using the shared dependency contract; AOR_SKIP_GATEWAY_SETUP=1 opts out. Existing services require restart after installation.

Default controller Gateway URL uses port 8787. Start Gateways separately from the main API/manual/console launcher. Pairing reset preserves TLS identity and must use the same account/state directory as the Gateway. See the installation page and macOS guide for supported commands and platform requirements. Never copy tokens, private keys or parameter values into diagnostics.

Correlated blocker cancellation accepts a job identity, not a caller-supplied PID. Active detached workers retain their cancellation watcher. Foreground executions use the registered executor; POSIX orphans are signalled only after creation-time, process-group and session verification. Windows orphan descendant termination is not inferred from a dead parent and remains unobservable when no active executor can establish control. No live production restart is required to clear stale rows once the upgraded Gateway is installed; source/package deployment itself still requires the supported installation and coordinated process restart.

Desktop publishes independent process, application and window capability tags from live native backend probes. See Desktop control for platform permissions and effect truth.

Host capability facts and process observations

Platform vocabulary normalizes recognized Linux/macOS/Windows aliases and retains unknown for other values. A label is not a capability test. Capability observations also remain separate from tool permissions and the accepted execution target.

Archive discovery locates 7z, 7zz, 7za, 7zr, rar and unrar. It runs only their explicit info/help argv with no shell, a 0.5-second timeout and discarded stdin/stderr. Captured stdout over 64 KiB is rejected after capture. Parsed per-format facts distinguish read, extract, create and verify: a 7-Zip reader does not imply RAR creation or integrity-test support, and UNRAR does not create RAR archives. Absent tools are unsupported; malformed or missing evidence remains unknown. Only allowlisted fields reach persisted/model snapshots.

The 32-entry process cache is keyed by executable and adjacent 7z codec stat identities; executable identity is rechecked after a probe. Returned facts are deep copies. Changes hidden behind a launcher/plugin require a Gateway restart. No archive content, installation or privilege escalation participates in discovery.

Plotting readiness instead caches local package versions, recorded installer failures and an existing browser executable. Its modes are independent:

Mode Observed requirements
Matplotlib PNG NumPy, pandas and Matplotlib, without a recorded Matplotlib render failure
Plotly HTML Plotly
Plotly PNG Plotly, Kaleido and an executable browser, without a recorded export failure

BROWSER_PATH takes precedence during browser lookup. These checks launch no browser or render; the operation can still fail later. Restart/cache invalidation is required to refresh this process-local observation after dependency changes.

Process identity compares PID plus exact creation identity. macOS uses the kernel identity for current records; a legacy wall-clock mismatch remains unknown rather than proving death. Socket admission additionally matches OS-reported local/remote TCP tuples to that process. Inaccessible evidence fails closed. Native Windows ACL checks restrict state-file grants to the current user and LocalSystem; they are separate from socket/process identity and require native OS qualification.

Telemetry rechecks command identity around sampling. RSS and IO describe the root process; CPU includes its available waited-child counters and at most 64 sampled live descendants. Child enumeration and membership can change, and inaccessible optional metrics are omitted. These diagnostics cannot prove progress, termination or external-effect completion.

Resource observations accept a much narrower evidence contract: explicit operands of simple file mutation/read commands, after the physical claim is released. Correlated read evidence must belong to the candidate's run, start after rejection and cover the known written paths. Direct inspection observes at most 64 paths with lstat; absent, inaccessible and opaque scope remain distinct. Present filesystem state never rewrites the historical command's exit outcome or authorizes a replay.

Inbound application, configuration and streams

The shared HTTPS launcher selects the instance before loading settings or creating TLS identity. It clears the settings cache, loads effective configuration, prepares the retained certificate/key and starts Uvicorn with ASGI lifespan enabled. Bind arguments and environment variables supply startup defaults; saved managed values can supersede them. The launcher fixture verifies this with an injected Uvicorn call, without opening a listener.

Settings validates ports, timing limits and working-directory existence, normalizes host-platform facts and combines baseline capability tags. A direct Settings(...) object supplies bootstrap configuration; get_settings() applies managed overrides and caches the result. Actual optional capabilities still depend on the service's runtime probes.

ConfigurationService exposes strict get, validate, update and reset requests through the shared managed-settings owner. Reads distinguish startup defaults, saved/effective values and the active process. Updates and resets require the observed revision. Validation previews a candidate without saving it, and reset removes selected overrides (all editable ones when no keys are supplied). Neither saving nor resetting changes existing service instances; restart loads the new effective configuration. Node identity, storage roots and derived platform identity are excluded from ordinary patches. The browser CDP endpoint is treated as secret configuration. The restart configuration test checks save, retained active settings, reload and reset using temporary state.

Platform modules export a LazyApplication. Importing the proxy does not construct its default services. Its first ASGI call or forwarded attribute access runs the factory under a mutex; successful creation is cached, while a failed factory call can be retried. Calling create_app(settings) explicitly creates a separately configured application immediately.

The application factory constructs GatewayService, restores jobs/worker communication, binds controller authorization and registers typed routes. Its lifespan then holds the shared state lease, starts artifact maintenance and the update supervisor, and closes those owners and browser/UI, mail staging, transfers and the job hub on exit. The state lease blocks an exclusive local reset while the application runs; the job hub's separate leases prevent duplicate authority. Shutdown is an ordered sequence of service close calls, not proof that every independently owned host process has stopped.

Authentication middleware runs before protected route dispatch. Public GET /healthz is intercepted there and returns minimal status; it does not expose the typed internal health response or prove authenticated execution readiness. The special update probe is described in local update admission. Private operation validation omits submitted input values. Jobs return their structured invalid-request receipt, sensitive routes return generic detail, and other validation responses contain bounded, redacted location/type/message fields.

Transport surface Response and ownership contract
Typed operation routes Validate requests and delegate to the service/provider. Node checks, host effects and operation receipts remain with those owners.
/jobs Preserves the receipt and maps unavailable runtime/control to HTTP 503, missing jobs to 404 and invalid requests to 400. Other domain errors can use HTTP 200; inspect the receipt.
Command SSE Encodes typed service observations. Ordinary stream failures emit an error event after streaming begins; that event cannot establish that nothing executed. Privileged stream wrappers close their service generator in finally.
/terminal/write and /terminal/input Write emits display output; input writes to the existing shell's stdin. They have different effects despite sharing a request model.
/terminal/ws Relays terminal events and typed input/resize/close messages. Disconnect cancels the socket sender; an explicit close message closes the terminal session here.
/jobs/events Offers optional bounded observation replay. It does not replace authenticated job inspection or completion receipts.

The job event stream permits eight subscribers. It validates a decimal unsigned 64-bit cursor and an epoch of at most 64 characters, sends an initial hello, and signals gap when the requested epoch/cursor falls outside retained history. Consumers must then refresh authoritative state. Events are filtered by job access, and the cursor advances past filtered entries. Pairing-revision changes end the subscription; idle waits are bounded to 15 seconds with heartbeats. Generator exit returns the subscriber slot. The hub's ring retention is documented under publication and authority.

The route-authentication tests check the registered surface inventory, rejection before dispatch and authenticated diagnostics. These isolated checks do not certify every streaming disconnect or native-platform terminal behavior.

Shared host-operation service

GatewayService is the common operation owner behind the inbound application and outbound dispatcher. Construction validates core runtime dependencies, restores the jobs hub and opens worker communication. It then composes file, transfer, document, device, browser, mail, HTTP and inference providers. Office, PDF and transfer operations share the file provider's mutation lock; local inference and GPU management share model-runtime coordination. Application/outbound lifespans own maintenance startup and service teardown.

Target validation has two forms. The common _ensure_node_matches helper follows the execution identity guard policy and emits an explicit pre-execution rejection marker when enforced. Typed Local AI, Docker, PDF, Office, GPU, Clipboard, Browser, UI, Screen and Desktop methods additionally compare the exact node directly. Disabling a shared guard does not disable those explicit provider-boundary checks. The artifact_use wrapper marks the lifetime of operations that can use artifacts, so maintenance can account for active use; each provider still owns containment and mutation rules.

Job admission resolves the working directory on the Gateway. For commands classified as mutations, the service derives conflict scope from its own node and resolved directory instead of trusting a caller-supplied scope. Existing job inspection/control also checks controller access. These checks precede delegation to GatewayJobs, which owns reservation, execution and reconciliation.

Failure boundary Receipt meaning
Invalid target, empty command or invalid startup directory Rejected before entering job start; no process is inferred to have run.
Job start returns its own receipt Preserve the job owner's phase facts, including a definite reservation failure or an uncertain launch.
An unexpected exception escapes the delegated start Retain an uncertain outcome because this boundary cannot prove where execution stopped.
Existing job control becomes unavailable Retain unresolved job state. TTY input distinguishes rejected delivery from unknown delivery using its delivery ID.
Private HTTP preparation fails before dispatch Return a generic runtime/profile failure without private exception text or an invented remote effect.
HTTP execution fails after dispatch Preserve authentication/resource dispatch facts; a dispatched resource write remains uncertain.

Foreground command paths combine the request's execution ceiling with a positive Gateway timeout, taking the stricter bound. Disabling operation-limit enforcement removes that timeout; optional Agent Check observation records threshold crossings without imposing it. Timed-out receipts retain the effective Gateway limit. Accepted SSH/Kubernetes/SLURM setup observations accompany real execution, and explicit Git observations are attached afterward; see command working context for their owners and limits. None of these observations replays the command.

The legacy /llm/* interface retains one process-local operator command, log path and owner. It is separate from typed Local AI profiles. Legacy start creates a process session and records a process fence; it reports starting without checking model readiness. Log reads default to 64 KiB, clamp to 1–256 KiB and return byte cursors; offset zero tails a larger file. Stop retains the owner metadata so status and logs remain available. The retained process handle does not become an automatically restored model owner after replacement.

Restart serializes with model lifecycle changes. It refuses live typed owners and legacy processes, including a surviving legacy POSIX process group after its launch shell exits. Once normal replacement is scheduled, legacy start is blocked until the process is replaced. An injected restart callback used by fixtures has separate cleanup of that pending flag. A restart acknowledgement does not certify the next process's readiness or the completion of independent jobs.

The isolated restart checks, HTTP boundary checks, directory checks and job admission checks exercise these boundaries with injected failures and controlled owners. Their broader suites also contain execution scenarios; a selected boundary check alone does not establish every platform or workload outcome.

Persistent terminals and managed TTY jobs

There are two terminal owners, with different lifetimes and completion paths.

Surface Owner and platform State and outcome
Persistent interactive session terminal facade selects POSIX sessions; the Windows provider rejects this interface Shell, CWD, events and capture registry live in the Gateway process
Command-owned TTY job tty_process.py selects POSIX PTY or native Windows ConPTY One command belongs to its job/worker; observations and input receipts travel through the job protocol

Persistent session capture and input

Creating a session validates its initial target-local directory and starts the configured shell with Bash-style no-profile/no-rc interactive arguments. Reusing a live session resizes it and preserves its current directory. Acquisition also cleans dead or idle sessions; this module has no independent expiry timer. Prompt control markers update CWD observations. Input writes UTF-8 to the shell; runtime-authored display output takes a separate path and does not feed stdin.

A session permits one agent capture at a time. Capture writes a private script with unique start/end markers, runs the requested command in a subshell, and reports the exit value from its completed marker line. Subshell directory or environment changes do not rewrite the persistent parent shell. The wrapper sets noninteractive pager/editor defaults while retaining terminal IO, and keeps its completion trailer in the script so a prompting child cannot consume the trailer as input. Uncaptured submission writes command text directly into the existing shell and returns without an agent capture receipt.

The parser handles split command markers and forwards prompts without waiting for a newline. Authentication, confirmation and pager patterns inspect at most 1,600 normalized characters. An additional idle heuristic uses terminal-control output without a final newline. These hints can request user input; they do not prove a process is blocked or authorize supplying a secret. While input is required, capture defers its timeout check and repeats notices at five-second intervals. Input clears the hints; it does not extend the original deadline.

Captured progress has a 64-event queue that marks loss after overflow. Display events have a separate 1,000-item queue that drops old events when full. Consecutive display chunks are batched toward 32 KiB; one chunk can cross that target, and the combined display result carries only type/data. Neither queue is a durable output history. A session exit event also cannot substitute for a command-specific completion receipt.

Command-group ownership uses a locked control file shared by launch and cancellation. A cancellation arriving before launch writes a tombstone; after PID publication it sends TERM followed by KILL to that command group. Cancellation lookup requires a registered nonempty execution ID. Its acknowledgement is not independent proof of process exit; OS failure can leave cancellation outcome unknown. Timeout asks that cancellation path to stop work before emitting a timeout result.

Closing the capture iterator releases capture bookkeeping and schedules temporary file cleanup after five seconds; it does not independently terminate the command. Closing the session terminates the persistent shell group. Captured commands have their own group and cancellation path. Session connection loss, command cancellation and shell closure therefore remain separate events.

Managed TTY process and input receipts

TTY jobs advertise tty_jobs_v1 only when the native backend is available. The POSIX adapter creates a controlling terminal in a fresh helper, avoiding thread-unsafe pre-exec callbacks. A notification byte followed by exec-triggered EOF distinguishes successful exec from helper startup failure. Windows creates a ConPTY child suspended, assigns a kill-on-close Job Object, then resumes it; this provides command-family ownership before the supplied command runs. Windows console closure uses a separate thread so output can continue draining.

The shared stream owner uses the managed temporary-directory supervisor and distinguishes process creation from its readiness receipt. A reader performs incremental UTF-8 decoding into a 64-item queue with backpressure. PTY stdout and stderr form one combined stream. Cancellation and deadlines terminate the owned process, then drain bounded final output. Descendants retaining an output handle cannot keep a finished parent open indefinitely: after one second of observed parent exit the owner requests termination and can mark truncated output. Final cleanup detaches input, terminates/reaps any remaining child and closes process, console and readiness resources.

Input defaults to appending Enter (CR) unless the supplied text already ends in CR/LF; raw mode preserves characters exactly. The limit is 4,096 characters including automatic Enter. Literal backslash sequences remain literal. The worker's InputWriter serializes writes and keeps up to 4,096 delivery receipts for its lifetime. The same ID and text hash returns the prior receipt; different text under that ID is rejected. It reserves an unknown receipt before writing bytes, loops over partial writes, and retains uncertainty plus the known byte count if writing fails. An unknown result must not be converted into a fresh unidentified retry. See the IPC input protocol for transport ownership and acknowledgement behavior.

Controller registry and observed health

AgentGatewayStore is the registry facade. Controller bootstrap registers its recovery path with the shared state hub; later callers receive the same MemoryGatewayStore. Normal reads use immutable RAM views and changes publish through transactions. SQLite initializes/imports recovery data and receives checkpoints. The standalone SQL implementation remains available when no hub owns the path; it does not supply the RAM implementation's transaction-wide management and stale-probe fences.

The registry keeps several kinds of information together, with separate meanings:

Information Owner and meaning
ID, nickname, endpoint, node and enabled state Saved controller configuration. A nickname is a display name; captured Gateway IDs select execution targets.
Configuration origin and insertion order Startup seeding adds missing stable IDs and preserves later edits. RAM node lookup prefers the requested origin, then retained insertion order.
Platform, capability tags and default directory Observations from a handshake or health check. They describe advertised support and are not proof that a future operation will succeed.
Public-key pin and enrollment counter Retained peer identity. Explicit reset clears trust and capability observations, increments enrollment and retains the profile.
Health and connection timestamps Latest recorded observation. Outbound health reads session presence locally; inbound health contacts the configured endpoint.

The default selector considers enabled records, preferring connected status, then startup configuration, nickname and ID. Resolving an exact node instead prefers its enabled configuration-origin registration. Neither fallback changes the captured Gateway IDs of an accepted run.

Management writes delegate to GatewayManagementService. In RAM, its update/delete guard executes inside the registry mutation transaction, so work accepted after Settings was loaded can still prevent an unsafe edit. Nickname uniqueness is checked there too. Editing scheme, host, port or node clears the previous capability observation. A nickname, working-directory or enabled-state edit retains the configured URL prefix. Endpoint edits do not silently replace an existing peer pin; trust recovery remains an explicit operation.

sequenceDiagram participant H as Health check participant R as Controller RAM registry participant G as Configured Gateway H->>R: Read endpoint, pin and enrollment H->>G: Verify transport and request capabilities Note over R: Reads and guarded edits can continue G-->>H: Capabilities or failure H->>R: Publish only if original target still matches R-->>H: Return current registration

Inbound health tries /capabilities; only HTTP 404/405 selects the legacy /healthz fallback. The fallback cannot establish modern capability support. Omitted capability tags retain previously negotiated support, but a default directory belongs to the latest successful observation and is not carried forward when that observation omits it. Failed checks retain the registration and prior capability evidence, recording an offline observation and classified error. An already blocked identity or disabled registration reports that reachability was not checked. A health timeout is not evidence that existing remote work stopped.

Network calls run outside RAM transactions. Before publishing a result, the store compares endpoint, node, enabled/transport state, enrollment and pin with the original record. A probe that finishes after a target edit cannot overwrite the new registration. TLS capture performs its own atomic pin/enrollment checks and commits an identity-change block before raising. Outbound hello publication revalidates the authenticated pin in its transaction; the public connection route requires proof before invoking that path.

The isolated RAM registry tests, management tests and health-message tests cover concurrent labels, delayed observations, checkpoint restoration, dependency races and the distinction between trust and reachability failures. See Gateway state and recovery for the separate authority on the Gateway host, and update coordination for maintenance holds on controller registrations.

Outbound connection and request lifetime

Use outbound mode when the Gateway can reach the Server but cannot accept inbound connections. The outbound client opens the Server's /api/agent/gateways/connect/ws route and dispatches requests through the same host service. It starts no inbound HTTP listener.

Before connecting:

  1. Enable the Server's HTTPS listener using its supported launcher and certificate configuration; see installation and startup.
  2. Create an enabled Gateway registration on the Server with the Gateway's exact logical node. An offline registration can be saved before connection; a node string in an unsolicited hello cannot create trusted authority.
  3. Set the Gateway's Server address/port and select https with --server-scheme on POSIX or -ServerScheme on Windows. The environment equivalent is GATEWAY_SERVER_SCHEME=https. Check saved managed configuration if the effective target differs from startup defaults.

The runtime requires WSS even on loopback. The launchers' retained http default does not make plaintext outbound control usable. TLS capture pins the explicitly configured Server, the operational socket checks that pin, and signed mutual proofs bind Gateway identity, controller identity, nonces and capability metadata. Dispatch begins after authentication and hello_ack. The transport predicate recognizes an outbound credential transport only when WSS, verified Gateway identity and controller authentication are all present; each operation's permission and credential rules still apply.

The client keeps a shared state lease throughout its reconnect loop, including disconnected periods. Failed connections wait from one second up to a 30-second exponential cap, with up to 0.25 seconds of jitter. A normally ended session resets the delay. Cancellation exits the loop. Connections disable proxy discovery, use 20-second ping/timeout settings and accept WebSocket messages up to 16 MiB; individual payload contracts impose their own bounds.

Each accepted request becomes an independent task inheriting the authenticated pairing context. Runtime/update admission checks its path, epoch and payload before service dispatch. Closing the session resets the receiver's context; it does not itself cancel every dispatched request or prove remote work stopped. Operation owners and retained receipts determine cancellation, completion and reconciliation.

Wire message Dispatch and result contract
JSON control Route-specific typed validation delegates to the shared service. Ordinary successful dispatch sends a correlated response with status 200, including job receipts whose body describes a domain error.
Binary transfer Only binary POST /transfer/chunk requests are accepted. JSON cannot impersonate that route, and binary frames cannot invoke other operations. Responses with byte content use the binary encoder.
Command/terminal stream A worker thread advances the service iterator. The client sends correlated stream_event frames, then stream_end, or a stream_error carrying the observed failure. The iterator closes in finally.
Agent Check observations Travel beside response bodies or stream events, preserving business/file content separately from policy diagnostics.

A send lock serializes complete frames from concurrent request tasks. Malformed JSON is skipped; malformed binary framing closes the connection with code 1008. Explicit HTTP-style service rejections retain their status and rejection marker; the listed private operation failures use generic error/uncertainty text. A failed send is a delivery failure and cannot establish that the operation was unexecuted. This dispatcher does not expose the inbound /terminal/ws or /jobs/events surfaces; terminal commands and job inspection use its supported request paths.

Loop teardown closes the updater, browser, UI and transfer provider, then stops artifact maintenance. Other resources retain their separate owners; this block does not close the jobs hub or mail staging stores. Process exit and local recovery therefore remain distinct from the socket's lifecycle.

Selected policy round-trip checks, binary framing checks and handshake checks exercise correlation, private invalid requests, replay rejection and transport verification with synthetic sockets. They do not qualify production reconnect timing or every native-platform shutdown path.

Transport identity and request authentication

Gateway TLS identity, controller pairing and operation permission have separate owners. tls_identity.py retains the Gateway RSA key and renews its self-signed certificate with that same key. Pins identify the public key, so ordinary certificate renewal does not create a new identity. pinned_tls.py captures a configured peer's identity on a TLS-only connection; operational connections verify their own socket certificate before sending application headers or execution payloads. A scheme label such as https is not evidence that this verification succeeded.

pairing.py binds one controller public key to the Gateway through a signed challenge and response. The challenge includes the Gateway identity, timestamp, nonce and pairing revision. Enrollment checks that the locked record is still unpaired at that revision, preventing a second claimant from replacing an established controller. A missing or corrupt initialized pairing record fails closed. The local pairing-reset operation changes this enrollment record while retaining the Gateway identity; the broader connection-recovery reset has the scope documented in installation and startup.

For inbound operations, client_auth.py binds the HTTP method, exact path and query ordering, Gateway/controller identities, timestamp, nonce, body digest and optional runtime epoch into a signed proof. The acceptance window is 60 seconds; accepted nonces remain fenced for 125 seconds with a capacity of 16,384 records. Timestamp validation alone does not prevent replay.

sequenceDiagram participant C as Paired controller participant M as Gateway auth middleware participant A as Pairing and nonce authority participant O as Operation owner C->>M: Signed target, headers and exact body bytes M->>M: Verify proof, epoch, size and body digest M->>A: Recheck paired controller and consume nonce A-->>M: Controller identity and pairing revision M->>O: Verified body under runtime admission and policy O-->>C: Operation result or execution uncertainty

auth_middleware.py verifies the actual body before accepting replay state or dispatching protected operations. It spools ordinary uploads beyond 1 MiB, limits the total body to 64 MiB and gives each receive operation a 30-second deadline. Pairing bodies have a 16 KiB limit; binary transfer frames use the transfer protocol's separate bound. WebSocket handshakes bind an empty body. The public /healthz response and first-pairing routes are explicit exceptions; a public health response does not prove controller authorization. Pairing attempts are limited to 30 within the middleware's 60-second window.

After hashing an upload, the authority rechecks pairing before durably consuming the nonce. A reset during upload therefore cannot authorize the former controller. Controller identity and revision flow through request context to job ownership and dispatch. Nonce durability belongs to the Gateway safety fences. Operation permissions, resource admission and capability checks still apply after authentication. Errors after dispatch remain operation failures or uncertain effects; middleware must not relabel them as proof that nothing executed.

For outbound connections, outbound_tls.py pins the explicitly configured Server and verifies the live TLS socket before the WebSocket handshake. outbound_auth.py then completes mutual signed proofs over both nonces, identities and capabilities. The session owner begins request handling only after the proof and acknowledgement; a saved identity-change block is not cleared by reconnecting automatically.

On the controller, outbound authentication requires an existing configured node and verifies the signed capability exchange. The session registry replaces connections only for the same verified identity and fails waiters on the displaced session. Each stream has a 64-item observation queue and a 256 KiB serialized-item limit. Overflow ends that observation stream with an explicit error so a slow consumer cannot block the shared socket. A disconnect, timeout or observation overflow does not prove remote execution stopped and does not authorize replay. Cancellation and reconciliation remain with the operation's owner.

The isolated authentication tests exercise tampering, replay, enrollment races, default-closed routes and upload/reset boundaries. TLS tests use local sockets and synthetic responses for first-use capture, renewal, identity replacement, redirects and post-dispatch loss. They do not establish native-platform or production deployment certification.

One current diagnostic limitation remains in the controller's job-start preflight: an identity change discovered during capability refresh can be reported as gateway_unreachable instead of gateway_identity_changed. The corresponding job variant in the TLS regression suite fails with that category mismatch on both the documentation checkout and its unchanged starting revision. It still reports a pre-dispatch failure. Check the saved Gateway trust state and health diagnostic when investigating this message; a generic category does not establish that the peer's identity is acceptable.
